abstract: The management of allergic and immunologic diseases has long centered on symptom management rather than disease modification. Conventional pharmacotherapy controls manifestations of the immune dysregulation but does little to treat the underlying cause. Newer monoclonal and small molecule therapies target downstream effectors of the type 2 inflammatory cascade, and allergen immunotherapy, while disease-modifying, requires years of administration for effect. Nucleic acid therapies represent a different approach that intervenes at the level of genetic information itself, at the DNA, RNA, or protein-production step. This includes mRNA treatments that direct cells to produce therapeutic proteins or modify allergen-specific immune responses; antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs that selectively silence disease genes; adeno-associated viral vectors for sustained gene delivery; and CRISPR-based systems that permanently edit the genome. Several technologies have advanced to clinical proof of concept including a CRISPR gene-editing therapy (lonvoguran ziclumeran) that reduced hereditary angioedema attacks by 87% compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial. An inhaled DNAzyme targeting the intracellular transcription factor GATA3 attenuated allergen-induced late asthmatic responses by 34% in humans, and CD19 CAR-T cell therapy induced drug-free remission in severe autoimmune disease. As of 2025, 24 oligonucleotide therapeutics have received FDA approval, including donidalorsen, the first RNA-targeted prophylactic therapy approved for hereditary angioedema. This review examines each therapeutic technology, its mechanism and delivery strategy, and the evidence relevant to allergic and immunologic disease. Persistent challenges, including delivery beyond the liver, immune responses to viral vectors, and the need for long-term safety data, are addressed alongside a proposed integration with existing treatment paradigms.

abstract: EDP167 is a double-stranded small interfering RNA (siRNA) drug targeting angiopoietin-like 3 protein (ANGPTL3), which may bring benefits for patients with dyslipidemia conditions. This is a dose exploration study in Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH) patients to evaluate the efficacy and safety and pharmacokinetics (PK)/pharmacodynamics (PD) profiles of multiple EDP167 injections.
description: Angiopoietin-like 3 protein (ANGPTL3) is a key regulator of lipid metabolism. Clinical studies have shown that inhibition of ANGPTL3 could exert lipid-lowering effects in patients with dyslipidemia. EDP167 is a novel N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated siRNA therapeutic that selectively silences hepatic ANGPTL3 mRNA expression, offering a promising strategy for lipid lowering. This trial includes two phase, main study phase (including screening period and 24 weeks treatment period) and extension phase (including 6 months treatment period). In main study phase, patients with HoFH will be randomized into two dose cohorts (200mg and 300mg, 10 subjects each), receiving EDP167 injections on Day 1 and at Week 12. At Week 24 of the main study phase, subjects will be evaluated and enter the extension phase, receiving EDP167 injections at Month 0 and at Month 3. The follow-up will last till Month 6 in extension phase to evaluate the efficacy, safety, PK profile and PD effects (ANGPTL3, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol \[LDL-C\], triglyceride \[TG\], and other lipid parameters) in HoFH patients after multiple EDP167 injections.

abstract:
AIM: Epigenome editing permits locus-specific control of gene expression without intentionally changing the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence. This critical narrative perspective assesses the small direct dental evidence base, separates molecular target engagement from tissue repair and identifies experiments needed to judge therapeutic value.
METHODS: A focused narrative search examined PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception through September 17, 2026. Evidence was organised into five categories according to proximity to endodontic application. A reproducible PubMed verification search during revision identified 73 records and two unique studies eligible for the direct editing and programmable activation categories.
RESULTS: Direct evidence is limited to locus-specific editing in human dental pulp stem cells. The FK506-binding protein 5 (FKBP5) study demonstrated promoter acetylation in cultured cells (n = 3 for chromatin immunoprecipitation), without editor-mediated repair in vivo. The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) study reported greater dentine mineral density after transplantation of activated cells (n = 5 in the microcomputed tomography analysis; p < 0.05), although its controls could not isolate the contribution of gene activation. Broader dental studies support regulatory roles for DNA methylation, histone modification and RNA methylation. Studies outside dentistry demonstrate durable and, in selected systems, reversible epigenetic silencing in vivo. Major unresolved issues are direct pulp delivery, cell specificity, duration, off-target effects, biodistribution and long-term safety.
CONCLUSIONS: Epigenome editing could provide targeted control of reparative, regenerative and inflammatory responses in endodontics without intentional DNA sequence modification. Potential reversibility must be demonstrated for each target and editor. Current evidence supports mechanistic investigation; clinical development requires editor-attributable tissue benefit and an advantage over simpler interventions.

abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide and is associated with profound pathological remodeling at both the cellular and molecular levels. Beyond transcriptional changes, post-transcriptional regulation-including RNA splicing, modification, nuclear export, and degradation-significantly expands the complexity of the eukaryotic transcriptome. Among these processes, RNA degradation remains comparatively understudied in cardiovascular biology. Traditionally viewed primarily as a quality-control mechanism that removes aberrant transcripts, including those containing premature termination codons, RNA degradation is now increasingly recognized as an active regulatory process that controls RNA quality, transcript abundance, and ultimately gene expression under both physiological and pathological conditions. Multiple mechanisms regulate RNA stability and degradation, including nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, RNA modifications, RNA-binding proteins, and noncoding RNAs, particularly microRNAs. These pathways have been extensively implicated in biological and disease processes including cancer and inflammation, and emerging evidence highlights their importance in cardiovascular homeostasis and disease. In the heart, altered RNA stability and degradation contribute to the regulation of cardiac contractility, ion-channel homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory response. Recent advances in reporter-based RNA stability assays and metabolic RNA-labeling approaches have further enabled quantitative measurement of RNA degradation both in vitro and in vivo. In this review, we summarize the molecular mechanisms regulating RNA stability and degradation, discuss their emerging roles in cardiovascular physiology and disease, highlight recent technological advances for studying RNA turnover, and examine therapeutic strategies targeting RNA stability. Together, these advances establish RNA degradation as an important and potentially druggable target in CVD.

abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated (Cas) systems are transformative tools in biomedical research, enabling precise and programmable manipulation of genetic material. Originally identified as adaptive immune mechanisms in bacteria and archaea, CRISPR-Cas technologies have evolved into versatile platforms for genome editing, disease modeling, molecular diagnostics and therapeutic development. Their simplicity, efficiency and adaptability have accelerated applications across a wide range of human diseases, including inherited genetic disorders, infectious disease, cancer and immune-mediated conditions. The present review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular mechanisms, classification and evolution of CRISPR-Cas systems, with particular emphasis on their translational applications in modern medicine. The present review aimed to summarize advances in disease modeling, functional genomic screening, diagnostic platforms and therapeutic genome editing, as well as the clinical progress of CRISPR-based interventions, including ex vivo cell therapies and emerging in vivo gene editing approaches, while distinguishing their relative stages of clinical maturity. Beyond therapeutic opportunities, challenges continue to limit the widespread clinical implementation of CRISPR technologies. Key barriers include off-target genome modification, inefficient delivery to specific tissue, limitations in large-fragment genome editing, immunogenicity of bacterial-derived Cas proteins, manufacturing and scalability constraints and uncertainties regarding long-term safety. The present review aimed to summarize ethical and regulatory considerations associated with human genome editing. The present review highlighted both the promise and the remaining challenges of CRISPR-Cas systems. Continued progress in editing precision, delivery technology, safety assessment and regulatory governance will be essential for realizing the full clinical potential of genome editing therapies.

title: CRISPR-Cas in translational research: From molecular mechanisms to therapeutic applications in human disease (Review).

abstract: Atherosclerosis, which represents the predominant driver of global cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, is orchestrated by complex gene regulatory networks. The present review synthesizes how non‑coding RNAs (ncRNAs), namely microRNAs, long ncRNAs and circular RNAs, act as central regulators of atherosclerosis pathogenesis and explores their therapeutic potential. The present review systematically delineates the mechanistic roles of specific ncRNAs in governing core disease processes in atherosclerosis, including: i) Endothelial and smooth muscle cell dysfunction; ii) inflammatory cascades; iii) epigenetic reprogramming, encompassing DNA methylation, histone modifications and N6‑methyladenosine methylation; and iv) plaque destabilization. Furthermore, the present review explores ncRNA‑mediated intercellular crosstalk using extracellular vesicles and evaluates their utility as circulating diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers. The present review also critical analyses translational advancements of ncRNA‑based therapies, covering therapeutic strategies from RNA interference and antisense oligonucleotides to nanomaterial‑based delivery platforms for targeted plaque intervention. The present review also evaluates emerging technologies, such as CRISPR‑based systems, weighing their potential against current biological and technical challenges. The present review identifies key challenges for the translation of ncRNA‑based therapeutics and outlines a roadmap for integrating ncRNAs into the framework of precision cardiovascular medicine. Realizing the potential of ncRNA‑based therapies will require multidisciplinary coordination, robust clinical validation and a deeper understanding of the multifaceted biology of ncRNAs.

abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis IVA (MPS IVA; Morquio A syndrome) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (GALNS), in which current therapies incompletely correct skeletal disease because enzyme delivery to avascular cartilage is limited. We developed a dual-lineage ex vivo gene-editing strategy combining murine hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (mHSPCAAVS1) and rapidly expanding clonal human mesenchymal stem cells (REC-MSCs), using an integrase-defective lentiviral (IDLV) CRISPR/Cas9 platform designed to deliver a GALNS cassette to the AAVS1 safe-harbor locus. Nocodazole-mediated G2/M synchronization further increased GALNS output in HDR-competent conditions. Edited REC-MSCs showed supraphysiological GALNS production and secretion, and edited mHSPCAAVS1 reached approximately 13.9-fold wild-type activity; enhanced expression persisted at 30 days post-transduction. In non-contact transwell co-culture, edited REC-MSCs and edited mHSPCAAVS1 each increased GALNS activity in MPS IVA patient fibroblasts, and combined exposure produced the greatest correction, reducing lysosomal mass by ~36%, mono-sulfated keratan sulfate by ~54%, and mitochondrial superoxide toward wild-type levels at 30 days. Irradiated REC-MSC feeder layers supported 2.59-fold mHSPCAAVS1 expansion and a 1.96-fold higher proportion of EGFP-positive cells. Cross-correction was therefore achieved by each lineage and was greatest in combination, establishing a functional basis for in vivo evaluation of this dual-lineage strategy in MPS IVA.

abstract: Hereditary tyrosinemia type I (HT1) is a severe autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by mutations in the fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) gene, leading to progressive and often fatal liver injury. Currently, no curative therapy is available. Nitisinone (NTBC), an inhibitor of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), is the standard treatment for HT1; however, its efficacy during lactation has not been systematically evaluated in large animal models. In this study, a FAH knockout (FAH-KO) rabbit model was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology and was shown to faithfully recapitulate the characteristic hepatic and renal pathological features of human HT1. Using this translationally relevant model, we compared different NTBC administration strategies. Combined breastfeeding and oral NTBC treatment achieved a survival rate of 87.5% over a 3-month observation period, whereas all offspring receiving NTBC exclusively through breast milk died within 15 days (P < 0.01). Under sustained NTBC maintenance therapy, FAH-KO rabbits survived, exhibited normal growth and development, reproduced successfully, and established stable Mendelian inheritance. Furthermore, we validated an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based metabolic reprogramming strategy. Hepatic portal vein delivery of HPD-targeting RNA interference via a self-complementary AAV vector achieved liver-specific HPD knockdown. A single scAAV-HPD administration rescued the lethal phenotype, restored liver and kidney biochemical parameters to near-normal levels, and supported sustained survival. Collectively, this study provides a robust HT1 rabbit model and proof-of-concept evidence for a long-lasting AAV-mediated therapeutic strategy.

abstract: Neonatal inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are genetic disorders that can cause severe, life-threatening manifestations during the early stages of life. Early diagnosis and prompt initiation of disease-specific treatment are critical for improving survival and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. This systematic review summarizes current evidence on emerging diagnostic and therapeutic paradigms for neonatal IEMs, emphasizing technological advances and clinical impact. Relevant reviews were systematically identified, and clinical studies evaluating diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for neonatal IEMs were searched in major biomedical databases. The evidence was synthesized narratively using a PRISMA-compliant methodology and assessed study quality and clinical applicability. Expanded newborn screening using tandem mass spectrometry has improved the early identification of several treatable IEMs. Emerging diagnostic approaches, including next-generation sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, artificial intelligence, and digital health-enabled clinical decision support, may improve diagnostic yield, particularly for ultra-rare and atypical presentations. Therapeutic advances include enzyme replacement therapy, gene therapy, substrate reduction, and precision nutritional strategies. Genome-editing approaches, particularly CRISPR-based technologies, also represent potential therapeutic strategies for selected monogenic IEMs, although these approaches remain largely investigational. Advances in screening, molecular diagnostics, computational approaches, and targeted therapies are expanding opportunities for the early diagnosis and management of neonatal IEMs. This review was not registered in advance, and the risk of bias was evaluated for each included study using design-appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Tools. Further clinical validation, equitable access to emerging technologies, and robust long-term outcome data are required to support their broader implementation in clinical practice.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: During the COVID-19 pandemic, lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have been widely deployed in clinical practice, demonstrating the clinical feasibility of this delivery platform. Although applications of LNPs in cancer treatment are advancing rapidly, barriers to clinical translation remain. Therefore, this review aims to summarize the major barriers and translational potential of LNP-based strategies in cancer treatment.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE for relevant literature on LNP design, formulation, and applications in anticancer drug delivery published up to May 2026, including preclinical studies, clinical trials, and reviews.
RESULTS: LNPs played pivotal roles in cancer treatment by delivering pharmaceutical ingredients, including chemotherapeutic and immunotherapeutic drugs. By encapsulating the anticancer medicines, LNPs facilitated drug delivery to tumor sites and protected the payloads from degradation in vivo. Major barriers include protein corona formation, inefficient endosomal escape, hepatic accumulation, formulation instability, immunogenicity and toxicity, and challenges in manufacturing consistency and cost control. Clinically, liposomal chemotherapeutics have achieved regulatory approval, whereas LNP-based nucleic acid therapies for cancer remain predominantly investigational. Moreover, structural modifications on the major components of LNPs helped address these limitations. The latest advancements of LNP designs and applications in the delivery of nucleic acids and chemotherapeutic drugs exhibited better biocompatibility and therapeutic efficacy with improved safety profiles.
CONCLUSION: LNP-based therapies hold potential for clinical applications in cancer treatment. Future efforts should focus on improving targeting and endosomal escape, reducing toxicity, and enhancing stability and manufacturing quality while controlling costs. Artificial intelligence-assisted design and biodegradable materials may support these developments and facilitate clinical translation.

abstract: Altered RNA metabolism and impaired proteostasis are central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). STAU1 is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein that regulates mRNA decay and trafficking, interacts with ATXN2, and is overabundant in neurodegenerative disease models. STAU1 overabundance activates mTOR signaling, impairs autophagy and stress-granule turnover, and thereby participates in a feed-forward circuit that further elevates STAU1 abundance. Here, we tested whether genetic and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated STAU1 lowering can interrupt this circuit in TDP-43-associated disease. Stau1 haploinsufficiency in Prp -TDP-43 Q331K mice improved motor performance and open-field measures, reduced TDP-43 and gliosis, normalized neuronal, apoptotic, and autophagy markers, restored TDP-43-dependent splicing, and attenuated transcriptomic abnormalities. Screening 2'- O -methoxyethyl (MOE) gapmer ASOs identified ASO-45, which lowered STAU1 in patient-derived fibroblasts and mouse CNS. Intracerebroventricular ASO-45 improved spinal-cord and motor-cortex phenotypes, restored splicing, and attenuated cortical transcriptomic abnormalities. In independent Thy1 -TDP-43 models, ASO-45 improved molecular markers and extended survival by 9.5-15.7%. These findings show that STAU1 lowering can disrupt a self-amplifying mTOR-autophagy-stress-granule axis and nominate STAU1-directed ASOs as a disease-modifying strategy for ALS/FTD.

abstract: Anti-CRISPR systems are emerging as essential regulators of CRISPR-Cas technologies, providing a controllable "off-switch" for genome editing, transcriptional regulation, and gene-drive applications. This review surveys the expanding landscape of anti-CRISPR strategies, including naturally occurring Acr proteins, engineered Acr switches, small-molecule inhibitors, and nucleic acid-based inhibitors. Acr proteins, discovered in phages and other mobile genetic elements, exploit diverse mechanisms such as blocking CRISPR-Cas complex assembly, preventing target DNA or RNA binding, or directly inhibiting catalysis. Recent work has revealed additional noncanonical mechanisms, including RNA mimicry, host-factor hijacking, and enzymatic modifications of Cas proteins. In parallel, computational screening and machine-learning methods have accelerated discovery of Acr families and enabled de novo design of Cas13 inhibitors. This review also examines engineered control systems that make Acr activity conditional on chemical, light, miRNA, protease, or other environmental cues, enabling spatial and temporal regulation of CRISPR function. Small-molecule inhibitors and nucleic-acid inhibitors offer complementary CRISPR control, including the potential for improved delivery, tunable dosing, and modular design, though further assessment in therapeutic applications is necessary. Across applications, anti-CRISPRs have shown utility in improving editing precision, reducing toxicity, constraining gene drives, controlling CRISPRi/CRISPRa systems, and enhancing safety in therapeutic and agricultural contexts. Despite substantial progress, important challenges remain, including delivery, specificity across natural and engineered CRISPR variants, and governance. Future efforts will likely focus on rational design, multiplexed inhibition, and integration of anti-CRISPR systems into existing CRISPR-Cas therapeutic and environmental frameworks. As CRISPR continues to expand beyond the laboratory into medicine, agriculture, and ecological engineering, anti-CRISPR technologies will play a central role in enabling safer and more precise genome engineering.

abstract: RNA editing is a post-transcriptional process that alters RNA nucleotide sequences, potentially affecting protein coding and RNA function. In this study, we identified 2132 senescence-associated RNA editing sites, defined as editing events present in highly senescent WI-38 fibroblasts at population doubling level (PDL) 50 but absent at earlier passages (PDL 20 or 25), by analyzing time-course bulk RNA-seq data from replicative senescence. Approximately 92% of these sites were located within Alu elements, predominantly in 3' untranslated regions (3' UTRs), suggesting widespread post-transcriptional regulatory remodeling during senescence. Numerous senescence-associated editing events exhibited elevated editing levels in tissues from older individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project. Among these events, F11 receptor (F11R) mRNA editing was observed across multiple tissues and exhibited higher editing levels in older individuals, showing a more consistent association with aging than F11R gene expression in human tissues. These findings reveal transcriptome-wide RNA editing patterns associated with cellular senescence and suggest that RNA editing may provide a complementary layer of molecular information for studying aging and senescence-related molecular changes.

abstract: This is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled, dose-ranging clinical trial to assess the safety and immunogenicity of novel influenza A Group 1 and influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine candidates given as intramuscular injections alone and in combination. A total of 60 healthy men and non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding women aged 18 through 59 years will be enrolled in one of 6 study arms. The 6 arms will consist of: 1) Sequential influenza A Group 1 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 (25 µg), 2) Sequential influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH4/3 (25 µg), 3) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (25 µg), 4) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 5) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 6) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and immunogenicity: 1) To assess the safety and reactogenicity of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products and 2) To describe the Group 1 and 2 anti-HA stalk IgG antibody responses of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products by ELISA.

abstract: Since its discovery, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) has revolutionized biomedical science and engineering with its ability to recognize and edit gene sequences with high specificity and precision. Despite the growing interest in using these capabilities to address environmental and sustainability challenges, the broader potential of CRISPR in environmental systems remains unexplored relative to its biomedical applications. Here, we provide a critical perspective on the emerging use of CRISPR for pollution management, ecological conservation, and environmental monitoring. Rather than viewing CRISPR solely as a gene-editing or biosensing technology, we consider both capabilities together to examine how advances in CRISPR engineering can translate into practical environmental solutions. We highlight the fundamental principles behind CRISPR-based editing and sensing and evaluate the challenges that constrain their transition from proof-of-concept experiments to field deployment, including off-target effects, delivery methods, ecological risks, and low sensitivity. Addressing these hurdles requires a multifaceted approach that integrates emerging technologies such as reversible CRISPR technology, amplification and cascade reactions, and machine learning, with strict regulatory oversight and rigorous risk assessments. This perspective identifies critical strengths, weaknesses, and research priorities for advancing CRISPR from laboratory technology toward robust tools for environmental applications.

abstract: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency (TFP-D) is a rare, life threatening long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorder caused by variants in either the HADHA or HADHB subunits, leading to toxic metabolite accumulation and systemic energy deficiency. Current dietary management strategies are only partially effective and fail to prevent long term morbidity and mortality. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) mediated mRNA replacement strategy to restore TFP function in a moderate severity TFP-D mouse model by delivering both Hadha and Hadhb mRNA. In cultured TFP-D mouse fibroblasts, dual mRNA delivery, but not single subunit replacement, rescued long-chain fatty acid oxidation and revealed a dominant negative effect exerted by the endogenous M404K variant Hadhb. In vivo , intravenous administration of dual mRNA-LNPs restored hepatic TFP expression, reduced circulating long-chain acylcarnitines, and improved physiological performance in aged TFP-D mice. Notably, intravenous delivery of dual mRNA LNPs significantly rescued cold tolerance test (CTT) performance by up to 71.6% compared to untreated and healthy controls. Together, these findings establish dual subunit LNP-mRNA delivery as a promising therapeutic strategy for TFP-D and support its potential applicability to other long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders.

abstract: This Phase II, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter study will evaluate the effects of lebrikizumab on airway eosinophilic inflammation in participants with uncontrolled asthma who are using inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment and a second controller medication. Enrolled participants will undergo a 3-week screening period during which assessments, including a bronchoscopy procedure, will be made. Participants will subsequently be randomized to receive lebrikizumab or placebo by subcutaneous (SC) injection on Day 1, Day 8, Week 4, and Week 8. Participants will continue their standard of care therapy throughout the study. End of treatment assessments will be taken at Week 12. Total study period, including screening and follow-up, is expected to last 23 weeks.

abstract: This is a 2-part, phase 1/2, open-label, multicenter study designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacogenomics, and efficacy of THT40 administered orally daily. This study consists of Phase 1 and Phase 2 components in subjects with advanced solid tumors and lymphoma with a focus on tumors with ARID1A and similar mutations who have progressed despite having received standard therapy or for whom no standard therapy exists.
description:
Phase 1 part of the study will consist of a dose-escalation and a dose-finding component. Phase 1 also includes expansion cohorts for subject with ARID1A and similar mutations.

Phase 2 will enroll subjects with locally advanced, recurrent, or metastatic, histologically confirmed advanced solid tumors or lymphoma, who have failed all standard therapies or for whom standard therapy does not exist, into 8 groups:

Group 1: Bladder cancer

Group 2: Breast cancer: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)

Group 3: Lung cancer (non-small cell lung cancer \[NSCLC\] and small cell lung cancer \[SCLC\])

Group 4: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and biliary tract cancer (BTC)

Group 5: Metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) including KRAS-mutated mCRC

Group 6: B-cell lymphoma including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)

Group 7: T-cell lymphoma (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma \[CTCL\] and peripheral T-cell lymphoma \[PTCL\])

Group 8: Basket cohort: tumor types that are suspected to have a related mechanism of action but are not included in previous groups including, esophageal, prostate, ovarian and pancreatic cancers

abstract:
This is a first-in-human clinical study to evaluate the safety, tolerability and efficacy of RXRG001 administered in the ducts of the parotid glands in adult patients with radiation-induced xerostomia (dry mouth) and hyposalivation (reduced saliva production).

In Part 1 of the study (open-label, single-arm), patients will receive unilateral administrations of RXRG001 in 3 single ascending dose cohorts and in 3 multiple ascending dose cohorts.

Part 2 of the study has a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Patients will receive bilateral administrations of RXRG001 in 3 multiple ascending dose cohorts.

abstract:
This is a single-center, open-label, randomized, dose-escalation Phase 1 trial evaluating the safety and tolerability of circRNA-HM2002 injection.

CircRNA-HM2002 (HM2002) is a covalently closed circular RNA, administered as an epicardial intramyocardial injection in combination with coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in patients with ischemic heart disease and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF \< 50%).

Two dose levels (5 mg and 30 mg per subject) will be studied sequentially. At each dose level, participants will be randomized 2:1 to the experimental group (HM2002 plus CABG) or the control group (CABG alone). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and tolerability and to explore the maximum tolerated dose (MTD); secondary and exploratory objectives include preliminary efficacy, peripheral blood pharmacokinetics, serum VEGF-A, immunogenicity, and biomarkers. Participants will complete a 14-day dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) observation period and be followed for at least 6 months .

outcomes.description:
The assessment covers 5 domains-physical limitation, anginal stability, anginal frequency, treatment satisfaction, and disease perception-to comprehensively evaluate the patient's angina-related health status during the past 4 weeks.

For each item, the 5 response options are scored with ordinal values starting at 1, where 1 corresponds to the response representing the lowest level of functioning. Item scores are summed within each of the 5 dimensions. Raw scores for each dimension are then transformed to a standard score: standard score = (observed score - minimum possible score for the dimension) × 100 / (maximum possible score - minimum possible score). The maximum score for each dimension is 100. Each dimension will be analyzed separately, and no composite score across the 5 dimensions will be calculated.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) can enable efficient delivery of mRNA for gene editing, making LNPs a promising vector for therapeutic treatment of inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs). Currently, LNP targeting of photoreceptors is inefficient and inconsistent between different cargos. We aimed to mimic the photoreceptor tropism of viral vectors by attaching adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid surface peptide derivatives to LNPs. We identified the most promising AAV capsid-derived peptides for photoreceptor uptake by confocal microscopy of retinal cross-sections. We generated LNP variants by surface conjugation of top performing peptides to maleimide-polyethylene glycol (PEG)-lipids. Peptide-conjugated LNPs delivered mRNA to photoreceptors and retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) in mice, with GS4, a peptide derived from the AAV9 capsid, as the top performer. Subretinal delivery of 1.0% peptide conjugated GS4-LNPs encapsulating Cre mRNA shows an 8.7-fold increase in photoreceptor transfection in the treated area compared to standard LNPs, respectively. However, when GS4-LNPs encapsulated Cas9 mRNA and sgAi9 editing was restricted to the RPE, reaching 10.9% editing of the total RPE and 31.3% editing within the treated area. Our novel GS4-LNP formulation demonstrates the feasibility for AAV peptide conjugation to LNPs and illuminates the bottlenecks in LNP-mRNA delivery to photoreceptors across mRNA payloads.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors (PARPi) are a mainstay therapy for homologous recombination (HR)-deficient cancers; however, resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Previously, through a genome wide CRISPR screen, we identified ZNF251 haploinsufficiency as a novel driver of PARPi resistance. In BRCA1 -mutant ( BRCA1 mut ) cells, ZNF251 deficiency led to HR hyperactivation, conferring PARPi resistance that could be reversed by RAD51 inhibition. In this study, we further show that ZNF251 deficiency induces replication stress and a pseudo-senescence state, in which cells exhibit molecular and phenotypic markers of senescence while retaining proliferative capacity. Because senomorphic and senolytic therapies can target senescent cells, we tested whether these approaches could overcome PARPi resistance in ZNF251 -deficient breast cancer cells. Critically, targeting this senescence-like state with either senomorphic agents, such as cytokine inhibitors, or senolytic agents, such as BCL-2 and BCL-XL inhibitors, overcame PARPi resistance ex vivo and in vivo . Importantly, pseudo-senescence was also observed in other PARPi-resistant contexts driven by HR hyperactivation, including 53BP1 - and Shieldin -mutant cells, suggesting that it may represent a broader mechanism underlying PARPi resistance in breast cancer. Furthermore, in two olaparib-resistant, BRCA mut triple-negative breast cancer organoid models, treatment with DT2216, a BCL-XL-targeting PROTAC, sensitized both models to olaparib. Together, our work defines a novel pathway linking HR hyperactivation, replication stress, and pseudo-senescence, and positions both senomorphic and senolytic therapies as promising strategies to overcome PARPi resistance in BRCA1 mut breast cancer.
HIGHLIGHTS: ZNF251 deficiency drives PARP inhibitor resistance through HR hyperactivation, replication stress, and pseudo-senescence in BRCA1 -mutant breast cancer. Senomorphic and senolytic therapies overcome PARP inhibitor resistance in vitro , in vivo , and in patient-derived organoid models. Pseudo-senescence represents a shared vulnerability of HR-hyperactivated PARPi-resistant cancers and can be therapeutically targeted.

abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1 , finding ∼50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1 -loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a (ARF) perturbastion altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten - and Rb1 -deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo .

abstract: Androgen receptor (AR)-mediated transcription drives prostate cancer progression and remains a critical therapeutic target. AR activation by androgens triggers nuclear translocation, DNA binding at AR regulatory elements (AREs), and transcription initiation. This process involves co-factors such as FOXA1, epigenetic modifications, and three-dimensional (3D) chromatin interactions. However, the temporal coordination of these events during AR-mediated transcription remains poorly understood. Using a time-course androgen stimulation model in prostate cancer cells, we first integrated temporal multi-omics data within the MOFA+/MEFISTO framework, which identified three distinct temporal factors underlying AR-mediated transcriptional dynamics, and then used higher-resolution early time-course profiling to further explore the chromatin and transcriptional context of these temporal patterns. Our combined analyses revealed that rapid AR binding at gene promoters, as early as 5 min, is crucial for initiating nascent transcription of AR target genes. We found that H3K27 acetylation at flanking AREs, pre-marked by constitutive FOXA1 binding, occurs prior to AR recruitment. Additionally, androgen stimulation induced a temporal early shift in nascent transcription from MYC to AR target genes, associated with transient disruption of 3D chromatin interactions. Finally, we showed that CRISPR-mediated inhibition of AR-associated chromatin contacts suppresses distal linked target genes, demonstrating that dynamic genome architecture is functionally required for AR-driven transcription. Together these findings uncover the dynamic reorganization of 3D chromatin structure and transcription factor binding post-androgen stimulation, resulting in distinct temporal epigenomic states.

title: Androgen stimulation rapidly reorganizes temporal 3D genome and epigenome states to trigger AR-mediated transcription in prostate cancer.

abstract: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is an Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-driven epithelial malignancy characterized by persistent viral antigens but inefficient antigen presentation, dysfunctional dendritic cells, and exhausted T cells. Although programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade has improved clinical outcomes, many patients do not achieve durable benefit. Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is an alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist used for sedation that was recently reported in a single preclinical study to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) through partial endoplasmic reticulum stress, eIF2α phosphorylation, autophagy, surface calreticulin exposure, and HMGB1 and ATP release, effects that enhanced dendritic-cell uptake and cooperated with PD-1 blockade in non-NPC tumor models. This phenotype requires approximately 600 μM DEX, several orders of magnitude above the concentration range in which DEX engages the alpha2-adrenoceptor selectively, so the effect more likely reflects an off-target interaction than canonical receptor pharmacology. We propose that, if independently reproduced in EBV-positive NPC and traced to a defined molecular target, this phenomenon could enhance cross-presentation of EBV antigens and prime EBV-specific CD8+ T cells, providing an immunological rationale for combination with PD-1 blockade. This hypothesis is constrained by the exposure gap, the absence of independent or NPC-specific validation, context-dependent tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive effects, a DEX-associated T-cell exhaustion signature, and the unresolved identity of the responsible target. We therefore do not advocate systemic dose escalation or immediate interventional testing. Instead, we present a staged falsification framework requiring independent confirmation of canonical ICD, spatially resolved demonstration of antigen-specific cross-presentation and stromal T-cell infiltration, deconvolution of the molecular target through thermal proteomics and CRISPR-based screening, and exclusion of hemodynamic, metastatic, and immunosuppressive liabilities before efficacy testing in EBV-relevant models. Only if these criteria are satisfied should localized delivery, target-directed inducer design, or prospective clinical evaluation be considered. This Perspective repositions DEX as a phenotypic probe for target discovery rather than a repurposed receptor agonist or an established anticancer therapy.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain.
HIGHLIGHTS: Biology : Chromatin and expression analyses reveal cell-type and developmental dynamics of brain disorder genes and variants. Atlas : Cell-type-resolved QTLs reveal dynamic genetic regulation during brain development. Mechanisms : Prenatal neuronal eQTLs implicate AHI1 in multiple sclerosis mechanisms. Therapy : CRISPR activation of an enhancer increases SOX5 mRNA and protein expression. Resource : BrainVar website enables interactive exploration of genetic regulation during brain development.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: SET binding protein 1 ( SETBP1 ) is recurrently mutated in high-risk myeloid malignancies, including myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap disorders (MDS/MPNs) and is associated with poor clinical outcomes. Although SETBP1 mutations promote self-renewal and HOX-driven transcription in murine and cell line models, the epigenetic dependencies sustaining these programs in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a targetable dependency in SETBP1 -mutant leukemia. Expression of SETBP1 D868N enhanced growth and serial replating of human HSPCs and established a transcriptionally permissive chromatin state, with increased H3K4me3, H3K27ac and KMT2A occupancy at SETBP1 -regulated loci. Integrated transcriptional and chromatin profiling defined a 94-gene SETBP1 regulome containing HOXA9, MEIS1, MECOM , and MYB and was enriched for transcriptional programs associated with KMT2A- rearranged, NUP98-HOXA9 , and NPM1 -mutant leukemias. CRISPR-Cas9 disruption revealed a functional requirement for KMT2A, but not for KMT2B or DOT1L in SETBP1 D868N HSPCs. Strikingly, deletion of the KMT2A cofactor MEN1 phenocopied KMT2A loss. Disruption of either KMT2A or MEN1 suppressed SETBP1 -driven proliferation and leukemogenic transcriptional programs, including leukemia stem cell-associated signatures. We next exploited this dependency pharmacologically. A KMT2A-MENIN inhibitor suppressed canonical SETBP1 target genes and abolished mutant SETBP1 -driven serial replating while promoting hematopoietic differentiation and reducing H3K4me3 at leukemogenic loci, despite modest effects on short-term proliferation. Most importantly, three clinically relevant KMT2A-MENIN interaction inhibitors impaired clonogenic growth across primary SETBP1 -mutant leukemia patient samples, while inducing myeloid differentiation and suppressing SETBP1 target gene expression. Together, these findings identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a key therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1 -mutant leukemia. The consistent activity of multiple MENIN inhibitors across a variety of SETBP1 -mutant patient samples and cell models validates the KMT2A-MENIN interaction as an actionable vulnerability and provides a strong rationale for expanding MENIN-directed therapies to SETBP1 -mutant myeloid malignancies.
KEYPOINTS: Mutant SETBP1 activates a KMT2A-MENIN-dependent leukemogenic transcriptional and chromatin program KMT2A-MENIN inhibition suppresses self-renewal and induces differentiation, exposing a therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1 -mutant leukemia.

abstract: RNA localization dictates where translation occurs, yet its disease role is unclear because most assays manipulate abundance, not position. We develop an optogenetic CRISPR-dCas13 system (Opto-CRISPR-TO) that repositions endogenous RNAs with subcellular precision, second-scale kinetics, and reversibility, enabling causal tests in vivo . In cells, Opto-CRISPR-TO routes diverse RNAs to organelles and ribonucleoprotein granules with multiplex, bidirectional control, revealing distinct RNA behaviors in centrosomes and P-bodies. In mouse retina, acute (4-hour) mislocalization of Actb mRNA redirects β-actin protein, remodels synaptic architecture and cell positioning, and persistently impairs vision. Thus, RNA location governs proteome topology and neural circuit output, and brief mislocalization drives lasting dysfunction. The approach generalizes across targets, compartments, and cell types, establishing a framework for probing RNA localization mechanisms in development, plasticity, and degeneration.

abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) sustain lifelong hematopoiesis, with developmental programs and the bone marrow niche governing their fate. However, how niche alterations and epigenetic dysregulation jointly contribute to malignant evolution remains incompletely understood. This article reviews HSCs origin and differentiation, with particular emphasis on the roles of endosteal, vascular, and perivascular niches. The regulatory mechanisms underlying stemness are examined through the lens of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methylation, histone modifications, and three-dimensional (3D) chromatin organization. The mechanisms by which abnormalities in DNA methyltransferase 3 alpha, tet methylcytosine dioxygenase 2, and additional sex combs like 1 promote the progression of clonal hematopoiesis toward myelodysplastic syndromes and acute myeloid leukemia are summarized. The review also discusses drug resistance and relapse mediated by leukemia stem cells, along with epigenetic- and niche-targeted therapeutic strategies. The review also evaluates strategies to improve existing DNA methyltransferase, enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), and histone deacetylases inhibitors. The review also explores rational combination approaches involving dual-function degraders, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and epigenetic immunomodulators, as well as emerging strategies based on transplantation, gene editing, and niche targeting. Moreover, the potential of single-cell multiomics and artificial intelligence is explored for enhancing clonal tracking, predicting resistance-associated mutations, and facilitating earlier therapeutic intervention. This framework offers insights into key disease-transition nodes and may help optimize therapeutic decision-making.

abstract: gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-Experiment-Assay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccine-related study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes. These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

abstract:
PURPOSE: Individualized mRNA neoantigen vaccines constitute a new pharmacological class of anticancer biologic, in which the drug substance is redesigned for every patient against the somatic mutations of their own tumour. This review appraises the molecular pharmacology, pharmaceutical development, cellular disposition and pharmacodynamic behaviour, dosing, drug interactions and toxicology of this class, and evaluates the evidence governing its integration into cancer chemotherapy strategy. No conventional pharmacokinetic dataset exists for any agent in this class, and no plasma concentration-time, clearance or exposure-response data have been reported; disposition is therefore described throughout at the level of lipid-nanoparticle biodistribution, transgene expression kinetics and immunological pharmacodynamics, and the title and terminology of this review have been framed accordingly.
METHODS: Narrative critical review conducted under a protocol registered on the Open Science Framework ( https://osf.io/8tgx4/ ). PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, SPORTDiscus and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to 10 September 2026, restricted to English-language reports, combining controlled vocabulary (MeSH: Cancer Vaccines; mRNA Vaccines; Antigens, Neoplasm; Immunotherapy) with free-text terms for neoantigen, neoepitope, mutanome, frameshift peptide, individualised neoantigen therapy, mRNA or RNA vaccine, lipid nanoparticle and immune checkpoint inhibitor, together with named-agent and named-trial searches. Reference lists of included reports were screened for further studies. A targeted update search restricted to the named agents and trials was performed on 2 November 2026 during revision. The search strategy, eligibility criteria, selection process and their limitations are reported in full in Sect. 2 and Table 1.
RESULTS: Neoantigen target selection remains pharmaceutically inefficient: fewer than 1 in 200 screened mutations is confirmed immunogenic, and consortium benchmarking found a positive predictive value of approximately 6% for epitope-prediction pipelines. Unlike small-molecule cytotoxics, these agents show no classical absorption-distribution-metabolism-excretion pharmacokinetics; disposition instead reflects lipid-nanoparticle biodistribution and transgene expression kinetics, with murine data indicating that CD8 + T-cell priming proceeds through a type I interferon-dependent cross-dressing pathway independent of conventional cDC1 cross-presentation. Clinically, intismeran autogene (1 mg intramuscularly every 3 weeks, up to 9 doses) combined with pembrolizumab produced a recurrence-free survival hazard ratio of 0.561 (95% CI 0.309-1.017; one-sided P = 0.053, a confidence interval that crosses unity) at primary analysis and 0.510 (95% CI 0.294-0.887) at five years in resected melanoma. The phase III INTerpath-001 trial (n = 1,137), reported in full at the 2026 ESMO Congress at a median follow-up of 24.6 months, reduced recurrence or death (RFS hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.45-0.75; P < 0.001; 24-month RFS 82.2% versus 70.0%) and distant metastasis or death (DMFS hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.45-0.85; P = 0.002), with overall survival immature (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.45-1.31). A prespecified piecewise analysis showed no effect in the first six months (RFS hazard ratio 0.99) and a large effect thereafter (0.42), the clearest clinical signature yet of a therapy that requires immune priming rather than immediate target engagement. Conversely, autogene cevumeran given as adjuvant monotherapy without checkpoint blockade was terminated in a randomized phase II colorectal trial for futility and an overall survival imbalance. Because these two programmes differ simultaneously in tumour type, delivery platform, patient selection and construct capacity as well as in the presence of checkpoint blockade, the contrast is associative and hypothesis-generating; concurrent checkpoint blockade is the most clinically tractable of several sufficient explanations, not an established requirement.
CONCLUSION: The pharmacology of this drug class appears to be context-dependent rather than construct-dependent: Clinical benefit appears to depend on disease context, treatment setting and combination strategy, although the relative contributions of these factors remain incompletely established. Rational incorporation into chemotherapy strategy will depend on pharmacogenomic patient selection, ctDNA-anchored pharmacodynamic endpoints, manufacturing timelines that outpace tumour evolution, and evidence-based combination partnering.

abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a secreted proprotein convertase that promotes lysosomal degradation of the hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), thereby reducing the clearance of circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). Its validation as a therapeutic target is supported by human genetic evidence demonstrating that loss-of-function variants are associated with lifelong reductions in LDL-C and protection against cardiovascular disease. This review examines the biology of PCSK9 and the expanding range of strategies for its pharmacological inhibition, integrating evidence from human genetic studies, clinical trials, and preclinical models, with particular emphasis on translational relevance. The monoclonal antibodies evolocumab and alirocumab substantially reduce LDL-C levels and cardiovascular risk, whereas inclisiran, a small interfering RNA (siRNA), achieves sustained suppression of hepatic PCSK9 synthesis with infrequent dosing. Recent therapeutic advances include the FDA approvals of lerodalcibep, a third-generation injectable PCSK9 inhibitor, and enlicitide decanoate, an orally administered macrocyclic peptide inhibitor. In parallel, nanoparticle-based delivery systems, active PCSK9 vaccination, and CRISPR-based genome editing represent emerging therapeutic strategies that remain largely in preclinical development. Beyond cardiovascular disease, PCSK9 has been implicated in sepsis, cancer, and neurodegenerative, pulmonary, and autoimmune disorders, although the supporting evidence remains heterogeneous and predominantly preclinical. In oncology, experimental findings implicating PCSK9 in tumor immune evasion and modulation of responses to immune checkpoint blockade have prompted its clinical evaluation as a potential adjunct to anticancer therapy. Further prospective clinical studies are required to establish the efficacy and long-term safety of novel PCSK9-targeted approaches and determine whether their therapeutic potential translates into meaningful clinical benefits.

title: PCSK9 Inhibition in Transition: From Established Treatments to Emerging Therapeutic Approaches.

abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are increasingly implicated in cancer treatment resistance, but the strength of evidence differs markedly among reported candidates. Because recent reviews have already catalogued circRNA biology, resistance mechanisms, and therapeutic applications, this narrative review focuses on how directly individual findings are linked to response to a defined anticancer treatment. Evidence is interpreted at four levels: human treatment-response data, direct in vivo resistance models, direct resistant cell-line models, and resistance-relevant biology without direct treatment testing. Direct treatment-resistance evidence includes circAKT3 in cisplatin resistance, hsa_circ_0007919 in gemcitabine resistance, circCDYL2 (hsa_circ_0004087) in trastuzumab resistance, and circRNA-SORE in sorafenib resistance. Experimental checkpoint-blockade studies also implicate circFGFR1 and circIGF2BP3 in reduced anti-PD-1 efficacy, although direct therapeutic resensitization by selective inhibition of these circRNAs was not established in the cited experiments. By contrast, several proposed links involving DNA repair, metabolism, stemness, or ferroptosis remain biologically plausible but have not been validated as treatment-resistance mechanisms. This distinction also changes biomarker interpretation: most tissue- or extracellular-vesicle-associated circRNAs should currently be regarded as candidate biomarkers of treatment response rather than clinically validated predictive biomarkers. We summarize the available human evidence, analytical requirements, and potential uses of longitudinal monitoring. Therapeutically, back-splice-junction-specific small interfering RNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, and RNA-targeting CRISPR systems can in principle suppress endogenous resistance-promoting circRNAs, whereas replacement approaches may restore sensitizing circRNAs. These endogenous-targeting strategies remain predominantly preclinical, whereas engineered circRNA therapeutics and cancer vaccines constitute a distinct platform that has begun early clinical development. Because the evidence base is dominated by preclinical models and small or retrospective clinical cohorts, with heterogeneous assays and endpoints, no circRNA discussed here should yet be considered a clinically validated predictive biomarker or an established resistance-reversal target.

title: Circular RNAs in Cancer Treatment Resistance: Evidence-Stratified Mechanisms, Candidate Biomarkers, and Resistance-Reversal Strategies.

abstract: Current lipid nanoparticle (LNP) optimisation and quality control frameworks suffer from a common limitation: they treat LNP formulations as morphologically uniform systems, obscuring single-particle structural heterogeneity. This opinion piece challenges the historical misconception that non-spherical, blebbed LNP architectures represent accidental manufacturing artefacts. Instead, we propose that the deliberate engineering of these non-equilibrium architectures represents a game-changing paradigm shift in RNA therapeutics. Consolidating emerging performance data, we argue that blebbed subpopulations yield enhancements in both in vitro and in vivo transfection potency. Blebbed LNPs may confer a particular advantage in difficult-to-transfect immune cell populations, thereby expanding their potential applications in immunotherapy and vaccine development. Mechanistically, this superior performance is proposed to be driven by the thermodynamic sequestration of ribonucleic acid (RNA) within the aqueous bleb compartment, shielding it from lipidation and degradation. Furthermore, we outline how bleb fraction can be prospectively engineered as a target product quality attribute using early-stage thermodynamic levers, specifically high-molarity kosmotropic buffers and delayed kinetic quenching under symmetric mixing conditions. To transition these architectures into a scalable clinical reality, we present a multi-parametric analytical roadmap combining automated, AI-enabled image analysis (LNP-MOD), cryogenic chemical mapping (Cryo-ToF-SIMS), high-resolution fractionation (AF4-SAXS), and single-particle loading quantification (NanoFCM, CLiC-ALEX). Crucially, we call for this analytical framework to be paired with biological validation across clinically relevant cell lines, prioritising immune cell populations to map subpopulation-specific trafficking. Ultimately, we advocate that specifying controlled morphological heterogeneity as a Critical Quality Attribute (CQA) managed during the manufacturing, storage and distribution stages is a true game-changer for the field. This framework has the potential to enable greater therapeutic potency, improve shelf-life, while also broadening global access to next-generation RNA medicine by reducing some of the logistical barriers often encountered in resource-limited settings.

title: Engineering and Analytics of Blebbed Lipid Nanoparticles for Next-Generation RNA Therapeutics.

abstract: mRNA vaccines established scalable manufacturing and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery for sequence-defined, non-integrating RNA medicines. In vivo CAR-T therapy repurposes this platform to generate CAR-positive lymphocytes after intravenous dosing, but its active product is a time-varying cell population rather than the injected RNA mass. This review critically examines the pharmacological sequence from biodistribution and cell-specific uptake to cytosolic RNA release, surface CAR expression, effector function, and disease response. The evidence comprises primary human T cells, mice, humanized mice, non-human primates, and 11 patients described in one correspondence and two meeting abstracts (as of July 2026). Matched studies show that receptor internalization can outweigh surface abundance, ligand density follows a non-monotonic relationship with delivery, and lipid chemistry and ligand presentation independently alter productive T-cell transfection. Preclinical models demonstrate transient CAR expression and target-cell depletion, whereas current human reports establish feasibility but not durable efficacy, a dose-response relationship, or the incidence of uncommon toxicities. We therefore distinguish administered dose, cell-resolved CAR-positive-cell exposure, and pharmacodynamic response, and propose their joint measurement as the basis for comparing platforms and selecting repeat-dose regimens.

title: From mRNA Vaccines to In Vivo CAR-T Therapy: RNA-LNP Design and the Pharmacology of CAR-Positive Cells.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have emerged as a powerful vaccination platform, yet efficient and targeted delivery of mRNA to professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) remains a major challenge. Here, we developed a dendritic cell (DC)-targeting virus-like particle (DVLP) platform for mRNA delivery by combining human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) Gag fused with the bacteriophage MS2 coat protein, which recognizes mRNA bearing MS2 stem-loop sequences and an engineered Sindbis virus glycoprotein mutant (SV-Gmt) that preferentially targets dendritic cells. African swine fever virus (ASFV) P30 was employed as a model antigen to evaluate platform performance. In vitro, SV-Gmt-pseudotyped VLPs encapsulating P30 mRNA (DVLP-P30) preferentially delivered antigen mRNA to dendritic cells compared with broad-tropic vesicular stomatitis virus G protein (VSV-G)-pseudotyped VLPs encapsulating P30 mRNA (VSV-G VLP-P30). In mice, vaccination with DVLP-P30 induced significantly higher P30-specific antibody responses than VSV-G VLP-P30. Enhanced humoral immunity was accompanied by increased frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory T cells, indicating improved generation of antigen-specific immune memory. Notably, DC-targeted mRNA delivery promoted stronger interferon-γ responses and increased IgG2a production, consistent with a Type 1 helper T cell (Th1)-skewed immune profile. Together, these findings demonstrate that DC-targeting VLPs function as effective mRNA carriers and enhance both the magnitude and quality of vaccine-induced immunity. This work establishes a versatile platform for targeted mRNA delivery and supports further development of DVLPs for prophylactic and therapeutic vaccination.

title: Dendritic cell-targeting virus-like particles as mRNA carriers induce Th1-skewed humoral and cellular immunity.

abstract: Introduction: Next-generation malaria vaccines are urgently needed to provide greater efficacy and longevity. Antibodies targeting blood-stage merozoites can confer protection against clinical malaria through multiple Fc-mediated functions. In particular, merozoite surface protein 2 (PfMSP2) is a known target of protective antibodies that can clear merozoites via multiple antibody Fc-mediated functions, making it a highly promising vaccine candidate. Methods: We developed PfMSP2 as a self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine, which was successfully validated for in vitro expression in mammalian cells. Subsequently, the PfMSP2-saRNA was formulated as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and evaluated for immunogenicity in mice following a three-dose regimen comparing 1 μg and 10 μg doses. We evaluated the induction of antibodies with functional activities relevant to protective immunity. Results: Our PfMSP2-saRNA vaccine induced antigen-specific IgG responses that recognised the surface of whole merozoites. Both 1 μg and 10 μg dosing regimens induced comparable antibodies to PfMSP2, and responses were predominantly murine cytophilic IgG subclasses. These vaccine-induced antibodies demonstrated potent Fc-mediated functions, including complement fixation and binding of human Fcγ-receptor I (FcγRI), after only two doses, which remained consistent after the third dose. Conclusions: PfMSP2 is highly immunogenic using the saRNA vaccine platform in a potential dose-sparing regimen, and induces antibodies with multiple Fc-mediated functions associated with protective immunity in humans. This saRNA platform is a promising strategy to develop highly efficacious vaccines requiring lower and fewer doses.

title: Evaluating a Potential Dose-Sparing Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccine for Induction of Functional Antibodies to Blood-Stage Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.

abstract: Therapy resistance in prostate cancer can emerge at different disease stages; castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is one clinically important state, and resistance to individual therapies may overlap but is not synonymous with CRPC. Metabolic reprogramming-including changes in glycolysis, de novo lipogenesis, glutamine metabolism, and mitochondrial homeostasis-has been implicated in prostate cancer progression and treatment resistance, although the strength of evidence varies across pathways and treatment settings. CircRNAs have been reported to modulate selected metabolic nodes in prostate cancer, although direct links between circRNA-associated metabolic changes and acquired therapy resistance are established only in a subset of studies. This review evaluates circRNAs as candidate regulators of selected metabolic processes in therapy-resistant prostate cancer. Mechanistically, individual circRNAs have been associated with selected metabolic changes through proposed miRNA-mediated interactions and, in some reports, peptide translation or protein scaffolding. These metabolic changes could, in principle, intersect with immunometabolic programmes such as lactate-associated suppression, lipid-linked macrophage states, and adenosine signalling; however, direct evidence that individual circRNAs control these immune-cell processes in CRPC remains limited, as detailed in the evidence tiers later in this review. Therapy-specific resistance networks are organised for enzalutamide/androgen deprivation therapy, docetaxel, PARP inhibitors and radiotherapy, distinguishing metabolism-dependent axes from signalling, mitotic, DNA-repair and exosome-propagated routes. Beyond mechanistic insights, circRNAs hold promise as non-invasive liquid-biopsy biomarkers and as druggable targets amenable to antisense oligonucleotide silencing, mimic delivery, and engineered circRNA vaccines. Major barriers to clinical translation include incomplete multi-therapy metabolic maps, sparse stage-resolved evidence across the hormone-sensitive→CRPC→neuroendocrine continuum, and unresolved delivery, safety, and regulatory challenges. Overall, current evidence supports circRNA-associated metabolic vulnerabilities as a promising preclinical research framework; however, circRNA-targeted metabolic interventions for therapy-resistant prostate cancer have not yet been clinically validated.

title: Circular RNAs in metabolic reprogramming and therapy resistance in prostate cancer: emerging links to the tumor immune microenvironment.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines offer a flexible approach to colorectal cancer (CRC) immunotherapy, with applications ranging from postoperative residual disease to metastatic cancer. This narrative review examines antigen selection, RNA engineering, nanodelivery, and clinical development, drawing on literature available through 21 October 2026. Tumor-associated antigens, shared driver mutations, and personalized neoantigens offer different advantages in population coverage, specificity, and manufacturing. Their activity also depends on RNA chemistry and carrier design, including lipid composition, endosomal release, APC targeting, tissue distribution, stability, and repeated dosing. Early clinical studies have demonstrated antigen-specific T-cell responses in selected patients, while randomized melanoma data provide a benchmark for combining vaccination with checkpoint blockade. The termination of the CRC adjuvant autogene cevumeran monotherapy trial highlights the difficulty of translating immune priming into recurrence prevention. Antigen heterogeneity, impaired HLA presentation, stromal exclusion, and liver-associated immune suppression remain important barriers in CRC. Advances in neoantigen prediction, self-amplifying RNA, and mechanism-based combinations may improve vaccine design, but their clinical value will depend on disease-specific trials that account for manufacturing feasibility and established oncological endpoints. The available evidence remains heterogeneous, with small CRC cohorts and limited randomized outcomes; the non-systematic search also introduces potential selection bias.

abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

abstract: Plasmacytoma variant translocation 1 (PVT1), a non-protein coding gene, is overexpressed in aggressive prostate cancer (PCa). Overexpression of PVT1 exon 9 has been demonstrated to induce malignant transformation of prostate epithelial cells and the development of aggressive PCa in vivo. However, the factors regulating overexpression and consequent oncogenicity of PVT1 exon 9 remain unclear. Here, we report the identification and functional characterization of a previously unrecognized internal regulatory element, the PVT1 exon 9 associated promoter (PEAP). We also demonstrate that its activity is governed by the caudal homeobox transcription factor CDX1 and local DNA methylation dynamics. While enzymatic methyl-sequence (EM-seq) profiling of PCa tissues and matched adjacent normal tissues revealed hypomethylation at PEAP in tumors, TFBind-based transcription factor motif prediction analysis revealed a discrete high-affinity CDX1 binding motif within PEAP. Using luciferase reporter assays, siRNA knockdown, CUT&RUN, CRISPR-based perturbation, isoform-specific droplet digital and quantitative PCR, we validated that the CDX1 motif within PEAP is functionally required for PEAP-driven induction of the oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 transcript. Moreover, CDX1 expression was significantly higher in aggressive PCa tissues compared to matched adjacent normal tissues in correlation with increased CDX1 occupancy at PEAP. Also, we uncovered enrichment of CDX1 at PEAP in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing PCa cell lines, and increased CDX1 expression across PCa models overexpressing PVT1 exon 9. Targeting the predicted CDX1 binding motif within PEAP with a custom-designed antisense oligonucleotide disrupted CDX1 occupancy at PEAP, significantly inhibited expression of PVT1 exon 9, PCa cell proliferation and migration. Together, these results define a novel CDX1-PEAP signaling axis in which promoter methylation modulates CDX1 access to an internal regulatory element at PVT1, driving oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 overexpression. This work uncovers a novel regulatory mechanism in aggressive PCa and highlights the CDX1-PEAP axis as a potentially targetable node for therapeutic intervention in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing aggressive PCa.

abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.
